### Title: Ask Yourself Nicely

### Content: 
When you want something from a stranger, you know you must be kind in making the ask. Of yourself, however, you demand instant performance. You lie awake at night, berating yourself: “Go back to sleep, you idiot!” Why not try what has worked flawlessly with other people for decades?
“Come on. Just another 30 minutes. Please? Pretty please? You can do it. I know you can.” Suddenly, falling asleep becomes a favor you do for yourself. You’re no longer an angry manager, trying to get an employee to perform. You’re a friend, trying to help another friend. The shift in perspective is profound.
Treat yourself like you would treat others. You’re a stranger too, you know? A stranger you happen to know well — and therefore must treat extra kindly.

### Title: Silent Acknowledgement

### Content: 
I can’t reply to every comment I get online. I can’t congratulate every friend on every LinkedIn update. These days, I sometimes can’t even answer every WhatsApp message.
But just because I don’t acknowledge everything that happens in my life does not mean I’m not grateful for it. I might not comment on your blog post, but I’ll still read it. I might not hit the like button, but I’ll still be happy for you.
Silent acknowledgement is a powerful form of respect. Don’t underestimate it.

### Title: The Backstory Is the Story

### Content: 
Tolkien’s Silmarillion is a masterpiece. Not because of how well it is written, how coherent the story, or how illustrious its characters. It is a work of genius because Tolkien actually took the time, thought, and care to craft 5,000 years of backstory to his main works, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.
The Silmarillion is the Bible of the Tolkien universe, and it’s not a book you read for fun. It’s a book you read to understand the world and the people in it a little better. To grasp the full meaning of the tales told in his other works.
It’s also a book you can read without ever having read or even heard of The Hobbit or The Lord of the Rings. That’s how good of a job Tolkien did. The backstory is a story in its own right.
Most of us don’t want to know the backstory. We want to know the result. We want the reward without the work. That’s why we turn on a movie on a Friday night, why we read a book in a weekend, and why we skim an article without ever giving it a proper read. We want the story without the backstory.
But the backstory is the story. That’s what the people who make things worth remembering know. They know that every piece of the puzzle matters, and that if you don’t put all the pieces in the right place, the puzzle will never come together. The picture will never form. And we, the audience, will never see the story that was meant to be.
It’s true that, often, the backstory will never be revealed. But that does not make it any less important. In fact, it makes it more important. If the backstory isn’t good, if it’s not coherent, if it doesn’t make sense, we will see right through it. We’ll know that the story is not a story at all, and we’ll toss it into the trash bin right then and there.
The backstory is the story. It is not optional. It is not something you can skip. The only question is whether you’ll tell it to us or not. But tell it to yourself? Craft it? Work on it? That you must do. You must do it for us. You must do it for yourself. And you must do it for the story that is meant to be.
If you don’t, no one else will do it for you. But if you do, you’ll give us a story worth remembering. You’ll give us a story that can last forever.

### Title: It’s Okay If the Glass Breaks

### Content: 
Donna Berzatto has been anything but a reliable mother to her three children. But when her only daughter Natalie, nicknamed “Sugar,” is about to give birth, the soon-to-be grandmother becomes an unexpected pillar of support.
 to-be mom, Donna says: “It’s okay if the glass breaks. You can always buy another one. And if you can’t, you can always drink from the cup.”
The glass Donna refers to is the one she smashed on the day of her own wedding. She was too nervous to go through with it, but her father reminded her that “the marriage is not the important part — it’s the wedding.”
Donna ran away and eloped with her fiancé, but on the day of the ceremony, she broke the glass tradition — a Jewish custom meant to symbolize the fragility of relationships — and thus managed to get everyone’s attention. It was her way of saying, “I’m not ready for this.”
Now, as her daughter is about to become a mother, Donna wants to make sure Sugar won’t make the same mistakes she did. “I don’t want you to feel trapped,” she tells her daughter. “You can always change your mind.”
When I started writing, I thought I would become a bestselling author within a year. When I started my first job, I thought I would be promoted within six months. And when I started my own business, I thought I’d make a million dollars within a year.
None of those things happened, and while I’m still working on all of them, I’ve learned that the glass always breaks sooner or later. The path to success is never a straight line, and so there’s no point in worrying about getting everything right the first time.
When you drop a glass, you can’t put it back together and use it as if nothing had happened. The pieces will never fit perfectly, and even if they do, the glass will never be as strong as it was before it broke. But even if you can’t use the same glass again, you can always buy another one. And if you can’t do that, you can always drink from the cup.
It’s okay if the glass breaks. Have the courage to admit when you’re wrong, and then find the strength to pick yourself up and try again.

### Title: Billion-Dollar Bullshit

### Content: 
From 2014 to 2017, Juicero collected a whopping $120 million in funding from venture capitalists. The company then applied “the Silicon Valley formula” to its product, a juice dispenser. They made a sleek-looking machine that pressed juice made of fresh, local ingredients from specifically designed and verified packets. They charged $400 for that machine. They launched exclusively in California and only sold to customers via a subscription model. And a few months later, they shut down and failed.
What went wrong? Well, the packets were neither fresh nor local. They came from a factory in Los Angeles and had to be shipped all over the place. The juice was nothing special either. It tasted good, but so does any juice. The subscription model, meanwhile, meant you were paying $5-$7 per glass of juice, and the machine itself was, well, unnecessary.
The Juicero machine was a $400 device to press juice bags with the force of two shopping carts. You could do the same thing with your bare hands, and in fact, people did. When Bloomberg published a video of people squeezing Juicero bags by hand, the company was toast. They refunded customers for months, then tried to sell the machines for $200, and a few months later, they closed up shop.
The Juicero is the perfect example of billion-dollar bullshit. It’s a product that solves no problem whatsoever, created by a company that does nothing but generate more expensive waste while claiming to do the opposite. Juicero’s founder, Doug Evans, was a walking, talking pile of bullshit too. He claimed he was “the Steve Jobs of juice” and that he had “a gift for juicing.” He also said he was “a raw food and plant-based diet advocate,” yet was seen eating a cheeseburger at McDonald’s. He also threw a hissy fit when the Bloomberg video came out, and he was a notorious bully at work, even physically attacking people on multiple occasions.
The Juicero story is a cautionary tale for entrepreneurs, investors, and customers alike. Don’t fall for bullshit, and don’t spread bullshit either. Don’t invest in companies that create problems instead of solving them, and don’t throw your money at solutions to problems you don’t have. If something sounds too good to be true, it probably is. And if someone claims to have a gift for juicing, you should probably take your business elsewhere.

### Title: Pretend It’s the Last Time

### Content: 
My sister once reminded me that there are plenty of last times we miss. The last time we hang out with a friend before our paths twist in separate directions. The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
’t worth torturing yourself over. But if you’re already sad about something you might lose before you actually lose it, you can flip the script. Instead of being sad, you can pretend the loss has already happened. Pretend it’s the last time.
When I’m sad about a plant that’s about to die, I take a picture of it. I spend some time with it. I acknowledge its beauty and its value. And then I pretend I’m already looking at a photo of a plant that’s no longer there. It’s a great way of getting closure in advance.
I can’t always tell when the last time is about to happen, but when I can, I try to savor it. The last time I eat a burger before leaving the US. The last time I’ll sleep in my bed before moving. The last time I see my sister before she moves to a new city. Those moments are worth etching into your memory.
The last time is always a good time to be present. It’s a chance to say goodbye properly. To remember what you love about what you’re about to lose, and to realize you can always love it again, even if it’s no longer there.
Don’t be sad about the last times you missed. Be grateful for the ones you can see coming. Pretend it’s the last time, and then make the most of it.

### Title: A Body Is Just a Shell

### Content: 
When his son Dino died at just 24 years old, the great Enzo Ferrari learned that engineers can’t fix bodies. In the world of Alita: Battle Angel, the opposite is true: With most people being at least partially cyborg, Dr. Dyson Ido, played by Christoph Waltz, repairs bodies all day long.
When Ido finds Alita, a fully cyborg girl with no memories, in a scrapyard, he initially wants to do the same. But the more he learns about her, the more he realizes that Alita is not just a body. She has a soul. A strong one. A soul that’s worth protecting.
Ido’s revelation is a powerful reminder: Bodies are just shells. We can swap them out. Replace them. Even abandon them. But our soul? That is ours to keep. We must protect it. Cherish it. And that’s why, when he first sees Alita’s head, hanging on a chain, Ido decides to help her. To give her a body. A shell. A new shell for a new life.
If you want to know what’s really important, look at the parts you can replace. Chances are, they’re not the ones that matter. Only once they’re gone will you see what’s left. What’s truly yours. And it’s probably a lot more than you imagined.

### Title: It’s Your Response-Ability

### Content: 
Sometimes, a word transforms completely when you see it not for its dictionary entry but for its parts. Will Smith is a master at this. So was Bruce Lee. In Striking Thoughts, he notes that “response-ability” is one of several synonyms for “living in the now” and leaning into your creativity.
’t be a more apt description of the word. Your response-ability is your ability to respond. It is a unique human skill, and it is what separates us from everything else on this planet. The word “response” even contains “sponse,” a synonym for “answer.” Your ability to answer is your power. It is a power you can use at all times, in all situations, and it is a power you can’t lose, no matter what happens to you.
You may not always be able to respond with your body, but you can always respond with your mind, and that is the truest form of response-ability. “The most important kind of freedom is to be what you really are,” Bruce wrote. “You trade your own reality for a role, for an act, and give up the one thing you possess: to create something better in your own life.”
There is nothing sadder than a human being who has stopped using their response-ability. Who has given up their freedom to create. They might be a prisoner, shackled in a dark basement, or they might be a rich heir, sitting in their mansion, feeling listless and bored. The former might have lost their physical freedom, the latter their mental freedom, but the result is the same: Both have given up their ability to respond, and that is why both are stuck.
If you’re a prisoner in a basement, you can still choose to be grateful that you’re alive. You can think about the good times you’ve had, and you can use your imagination to create a new, better reality. If you’re a bored millionaire, you can get up off your butt, go outside, and do something for others. You can choose to use your money to make a difference.
The point is that you always have a choice, and you can always use that choice to create. It might not always be the kind of creation you’d like to make, but it is a creation nonetheless, and it will always have value. Even if you can’t see it.
You have the ability to respond. You are response-able. Use it. Use it to make something better, not just for yourself but for everyone. That is your true calling, and it is one you can answer at all times.

### Title: Creativity as a Well

### Content: 
Sometimes, I happen to draft article ideas during my meditation, and sometimes, all 15 minutes of endurance training go to that activity. That’s not ideal, but it, too, teaches me a lesson: If I spend as little as a quarter of an hour brainstorming, thinking through the past 24 hours, about what happened this week, and allowing my mind to resurface whichever thought it prefers, I have article ideas out the wazoo.
In other words, creativity is like a well: If you go to it every day, you’ll never run out of water. In fact, if you go every day, you’ll likely pull up more water than you can use. This applies to any kind of creative endeavor, be it writing, painting, making music, or building a business.
It’s easy to feel as if you’re being unproductive when you’re brainstorming, thinking, or staring at a blank canvas. Actually, you’re doing the most important work you can do: refilling your well. Keep visiting it daily, and you’ll never thirst for inspiration again.

### Title: Dust Walls

### Content: 
A few weeks ago, I was scheduling dozens of posts from the blog to republish them elsewhere. Copy, paste, pick date, hit the button, repeat.
After I had done maybe 40 or so, I looked at the list of posts still left to schedule. There were 60 more to go. My heart sank. “Ugh. This is gonna be a long slog.” I would have to do this same, boring task two and a half times more still to get it done.
But then I remembered: “Wait a minute. This is just a list of posts. Nothing more, nothing less. It’s just a piece of paper. And on that piece of paper, there are 100 items. So what?”
The only thing that made that list daunting was the invisible cloud of dust surrounding it. The “I don’t wanna do this” aura. But if I could clear away the dust, I’d see it for what it is: just another task, like any other. In fact, I might even enjoy it.
I took a deep breath, started on the next item, and — you could almost see it — the cloud of dust settled on the floor. Suddenly, the task was easy. Fun, even. I cruised right through those 60 items. It was a piece of cake.
The only walls we have in our lives are the ones we build out of dust. If you feel stuck, chances are, you’ve surrounded yourself with dirt. You’ve psyched yourself out of the very thing you want to do.
Clear away the dust. Wash the walls. And remember: What feels like a big obstacle is often just a tiny speck of sand.

### Title: My First Job

### Content: 
That’s an odd phrase to type when you’re 33 years old. But I guess it is. Outside of some internships, only one of which lasted five months instead of just a few weeks, I’ve never held a full-time job—until now. “Business Course Writer.” That’s my title. My responsibility will be to create materials that’ll help enterprise employees understand blockchain and its applications. Kinda cool, huh? I’m definitely not complaining. Storytelling all the way!
I’m not sure how I ended up here, but it’s a good place to be. I’ve only been at it for two weeks, but I already love my new job. I love waking up at 7 AM. I love starting work at 8. My first job. How about that?

### Title: Still Water Is a Mirror

### Content: 
“Moving, be like water. Still, be like a mirror.” That’s one of Bruce Lee’s Striking Thoughts. When I read it, I realized that, actually, this is an encouragement to be like water, period.
’t’see it? Even when water is still, it’s still water. And when it’s still, it becomes a mirror.
When you’re moving, be like water. Adapt. Flow wherever you need to flow to get to where you want to go. Break down barriers, but only if you have to. Find the path of least resistance.
When you’re still, be like a mirror. Reflect. Look at yourself. What do you see? Do you like what you see? What needs to change? What must you remember? Which of your strengths will you need going forward?
Water is the epitome of balance. It can be the strongest force on earth, yet it’s also the softest. It can be still, yet always move. It can be a mirror, yet see everything. And it can be all these things at the same time.
Be like water.

### Title: Mapping the Terrain

### Content: 
“Where does that door lead again?” Confusion arose in yesterday’s gaming session. My girlfriend held the controller for The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom. As part of her turn, she had stormed headlong into a new dungeon. I kept asking her to backtrack, but that was not her style. “No, no, no, just keep going!”
In the end, we had to backtrack anyway, and we had to do it the hard way. We couldn’t go back through the door we had come from, but we could use the map to see where we had to go to get back to where we had already been. After we did, the path forward was clear — and the map was the star of the show.
I’m not sure how much time we saved, but I am sure we would have wasted hours without the map. It’s easy to get lost in a big world, be it the world of Hyrule or the world of a new job, relationship, or business venture. A map won’t always be available, but whenever you can, try to orient yourself before you set off. Mapping the terrain will rarely be a waste of time, and you’ll rarely find yourself in a dead end.

### Title: Remembering This

### Content: 
In 2014, I was an intern at BMW M in Munich. I lived in a tiny apartment offered by the company that somehow still cost almost my entire below-minimum-wage salary. I was young, relatively broke, and single.
’t wait to get out of there. I wanted a job, money, and a girlfriend. I wanted to go to London, Tokyo, and LA. I wanted a bigger apartment, a better job, and a faster car. I wanted, wanted, wanted.
In 2023, I was an intern at BMW M in Munich. I lived in a tiny apartment offered by the company that somehow still cost almost my entire below-minimum-wage salary. I was young, relatively broke, and single.
I was happy. I had a job, enough money, and a great group of friends. I could go to London, Tokyo, and LA any time. I had a cozy apartment, a fun job, and a great car. I was content, content, content.
The only difference? Remembering this.

### Title: Don’t Give Up in Anger What You Started in Love

### Content: 
The Silo is a dangerous place. 10,000 people cooped up in a 144-floor concrete pillar at all times, with no access to the outside? That’s a recipe for disaster even on the best of days. But once people start dying under mysterious circumstances, all bets are off.
’t ask for a better mystery than one in which the only detective is the prime suspect. That’s what Sherif Thompson is faced with in Harp, the latest entry in the Silo novels series by Hugh Howey.
When the mayor asks him to look into the case, Sherif isn’t exactly excited. He’s a widower, a single dad, and he’d much rather take care of his son Julius and go about his day than deal with the Silo’s petty politics. But he also can’t say no. Not to his old flame. Not to the woman who once saved his life. And so, against his better judgement, Sherif agrees.
As the investigation progresses, Sherif and the mayor’s relationship is rekindled. It’s been years since his wife died, and the mayor is a widow too. They both need company. But when the case takes a nasty turn, Sherif’s life is in danger, and the mayor must make a difficult decision: Will she sacrifice the man she loves to save the Silo?
In the end, she does, and Sherif is forced to flee. In the chaos that follows, the mayor must decide how to handle the situation. In a moment of quiet, she remembers Sherif’s words from the beginning of it all:
“I started this in love, and I want to finish it in love.”
The mayor realizes that, despite the mess he caused, she mustn’t give up in anger what she started in love. And so, instead of ordering a manhunt, she lets Sherif go. She’ll keep him close, but she won’t destroy him. And she won’t destroy their relationship either.
The next day, the mayor finds a note in her office. It’s from Sherif. It says: “I started this in love, and I finished it in love.” And then he’s gone.
When you start something in love, finish it in love. Don’t give up in anger what you began with passion. It’s okay to fail. It’s okay to lose. But don’t lose yourself over something that’s not your true self.
You can’t control what happens in life, but you can control what you choose to believe. Choose to believe in love, and, no matter what happens, you’ll always find your way back home.

### Title: Driving a T-Rex

### Content: 
I used to visit a friend’s house after school in the 90s. We played Need for Speed 2 on his computer. Thanks to a bunch of cheat codes, you could turn the game from a challenging car race into a completely ridiculous experience. I distinctly remember driving a T-rex around a Hollywood studios–inspired track at 200+ kilometers per hour. It was insane—but also insanely fun.
The game was already 20 years old, and yet, I still remember it. It’s a good example of what the internet has now coined “ a 10/10 experience.” Back then, we didn’t use that term. We just called it cool. Or awesome. Or epic. But we knew it when we saw it, and we had no problem gushing about it for minutes to our friends.
I’m not sure we do as much gushing these days. The internet has made it easy to criticize everything. There’s always someone pointing out what’s wrong with any experience, and they’ll do so in public. Often, they’ll get more attention than the people who had a positive experience and want to share it. That’s a shame, because if we only focus on what’s wrong, we’ll miss what’s right—and the right things are usually more important than the wrong ones.
When you see something cool, don’t hold your breath. Tell people. Don’t wait for the moment to pass. Don’t wait for someone else to do it. And don’t wait until you have a better story. You don’t need a funny anecdote. You don’t need a perfectly crafted tweet. You don’t need to be a car expert to say you enjoyed a car game.
When you see someone driving a T-rex, point at it and say: “Look! A T-rex!” You never know who might remember it 20 years later.

### Title: Big Waves Take Time

### Content: 
Let’s say you’re starting a job after ten years of self-employment. That’s a big shift. As you look back on a decade of work, you realize what felt like a trip through the jungle was actually baking a layer cake, with many artifacts now remaining. But what will you do with them? All those websites and email signup forms and social profiles.
You can’t just abandon everything. But you can’t keep doing everything either. You have a new job now! What are you gonna do? This is a big wave, and it will take a while to pass.
You’ll spend weeks thinking about it. You’ll have ideas. You’ll do some things and then undo them. You’ll let it sit for a while. And then, one day, you’ll wake up with a new structure in mind. You’ll spend days implementing it. You’ll feel good about it. And then, finally, you’ll be able to ride the wave.
Big waves take time. They needn’t wash you away.

### Title: Flick It Again

### Content: 
We have a big cuddle blanket on our couch. It’s massive. Two by two meters or so. In the winter, we use it every night, and every morning, I fold it back into shape.
’t easy. You can’t just fold a blanket like that. It’s too heavy. You’ll hurt your back. You have to flick it.
You grab one end, hold it high in the air, then let it fall onto the couch. It’ll settle in a straight line. You do that a few times, fold it over, and voilà, you have a nice, rectangular blanket ready to be placed in the right spot.
The hardest part of folding the blanket, however, is not flicking it. It’s starting over when you mess up. You can’t just flick it once. You have to flick it again. And again. And again.
This morning, I flicked the blanket, but it landed in a diagonal line. “Ugh. Alright, here we go.” I flicked it again. This time, it landed straight, but the edge was crooked. “Ugh. Alright, here we go.” I flicked it again.
The third time, it finally landed straight, and I could fold the blanket. But it’s that second “Ugh. Alright, here we go” that makes all the difference. If I don’t make that effort, the blanket will be crooked, and I’ll have to fold it again later.
It’s easy to give up when you don’t get it right the first time. It’s easy to say, “Good enough,” and move on. But if you care about something, you’ll flick it again. You’ll make the effort, and you’ll get it right.

### Title: Keep Pecking

### Content: 
I’m sick for the umpteenth time this year. I have to change my travel plans, again. There’s a lot of work to be worked through, and yet once more here I sit, upright in bed, doing what I can but mostly resting and passing the time.
’type’. It’s not the kind of typing I’d like to do, but it’s still typing. It’s the kind of typing that keeps me warm, keeps me sane, and keeps me in the game.
It’s easy to feel useless when you can’t do anything at full capacity. It’s easy to throw your hands up in the air and say, “I’ll try again tomorrow.” But even if you’re not a writer, you can still write. You can still send a few emails, make a few calls, and move a few things around on your Trello board. You can still send out a few job applications, plan your exercise routine for the week, or think about how you’ll tackle an important project once you’re back in the office.
When a woodpecker comes across a tree, it doesn’t start hammering away at full force. It pokes around. It taps here, taps there. “Is this where the insects are hiding? Or this? Aha, found some! Now, let’s get to work!”
When you’re not at your best, keep pecking. You may not find a big meal, but you’re still part of the game, and you’ll be back in full force soon enough.

### Title: An Eternity for a Steppenwolf

### Content: 
A “Steppenwolf” is a kind of wolfhound, half wild animal, half domesticated pet. In Hermann Hesse’s novel of the same name, protagonist Harry claims to be a specimen of this very variety, forever torn between a life outside society’s expectations and the comfort of hiding his lofty ideals in plain sight: among pubs, discussions about politics, and everything else mundane.
As a reader, I was shocked to discover that, at age 37, I might be a Steppenwolf myself. I’ve always had a penchant for the arts, and I’ve always felt out of place in most social circles, but I never thought of these as symptoms of a larger pattern. I was even more surprised to find out that Harry’s story is, by and large, the story of any artist, creator, or intellectual worth their salt. It’s a story of being misunderstood, of being an outcast, and of feeling lonely despite being surrounded by people.
It’s a story of being misunderstood, of being an outcast, and of feeling lonely despite being surrounded by people.
In one of the book’s many dialogues, Harry talks to his friend and mentor, a man named Pablo, who runs a jazz club. “I’m a Steppenwolf,” Harry claims. “I live outside the fence, on the edge of the world.” Pablo is unconvinced: “A Steppenwolf who reads Goethe! And who demonstrates, moreover, that he understands him. No, dear friend, you are not a Steppenwolf at all. A Steppenwolf would never have taken the trouble to read a single one of Goethe’s works carefully in order to pick up a quotation.”
While I’m sure Pablo has a point, I think there’s also something to be said for the Steppenwolf’s loneliness. After all, even Pablo, Harry’s closest friend, does not understand him. But what if that loneliness is not a bad thing? What if it’s a gift?
In one of the book’s climactic scenes, Harry gets to meet the “immortals,” a group of people who have lived for thousands of years. They are not literally immortal, but they are the souls of the greats who have lived before, like Mozart, Dante, and Goethe. “It’s a pity that you overheard me talking to Mozart,” the narrator, an unnamed representative of the group, tells Harry. “It has frightened you and you have made a wrong interpretation of it. But I can’t see why you should take it so badly. It’s not so odd, this meeting with the immortals, as you fancy it to be. It happens to many people who never get to hear of it and to many others who hear of it but don’t believe it.”
What follows is a little bit like a scene from The Matrix. The narrator explains that, like the people in the Matrix, most of us live our lives in a dream, a dream we can’t wake up from until we die. “You, however, call yourself a Steppenwolf, and are therefore obliged to believe that the things of everyday life are for you illusion. You have set yourself apart and dreamed, and in your dreams you have made yourself at home. But you are no more at home in your dreams than a bather is at home in the sea. You must get out. You must realize that your dreams are also just everyday happenings, just another form of reality, but one which you have with your eyes closed, while your real life, the life in which you are a material man, you have with your eyes open.”
The narrator goes on to explain that, unlike the people in the Matrix, we can wake up from our dreams. We can realize that our everyday lives are as real as our dreams, and that our dreams are as much a part of our lives as our waking hours. But there’s a catch: “You must learn to dream a better dream. The dream is always the same, always this nightmare within the prison, and it must be interpreted in the light of reality, that is to say of life’s ordinary happenings, with their meaning reversed. The dream is the mirror of reality, and our life is the dream of the immortals.”
In other words, the immortals are the ones dreaming, and we are the dream. We are the ones living the lives that the immortals dream about. And the only way for us to wake up from our dreams is to realize that we are the ones dreaming. We are the ones living the lives that the immortals dream about. ### Title: Helping Is a Decision

### Content: 
This morning, my girlfriend and I needed a quick snack before a big event. There were no bakeries near our hotel, and we didn’t have time for a full breakfast. When she went down and asked if we could purchase two croissants or so, the lady said: “Oh, just grab a plate and take whatever! No charge.”
That’s helping. It’s a decision. The hotel chain is a big one. They have a budget for “leftover food.” But it’s a budget they’ve allocated. Someone decided to put it there. And now, every employee can choose to help.
The lady at the front desk decided to help. She could have asked us to pay. She could have said they don’t have any pastries left. She chose to help.
Helping is a decision. You can make it any time. And you can choose to help in any way.
The easiest way to help is to ask: “How can I help?” But you don’t even have to do that. You can just help. Wave someone through in traffic. Hold the door. Give up your seat. Buy flowers. Surprise your kids with ice cream. Offer to take on a project.
Helping is a decision. Make it every day.

### Title: Life Is Not a Simulation

### Title: Appreciate the Basics

### Content: 
Today, our apartment has no water for eight hours. The irony? Outside, it’s raining all day long. But there’s a difference between water coming out of the sky or the ground and fresh H2O pouring out of your tap, and you only realize how big of a difference it is when you’re left without your usual conveniences.
’t drink tap water in Mexico, and so whenever I visit my girlfriend’s family, I’m once again reminded that, yes, clean water is worth a lot. Worth more, perhaps, than even its expensive-as-it-is price tag in Germany.
Appreciate the basics. You can’t do anything without them, and yet they’re the easiest to take for granted.

### Title: The Demand Was Just Too Big

### Content: 
The customer in front of me kept asking the barista about their café’s expansion. One tiny corner shop had turned into a three-room venue already, replete with a bakery and a space to give classes. Now, they had opened another, even bigger location elsewhere in town. How did they do it? All the barista could do was shrug: “Beats me. It’s such a saturated market. But the demand was just too big.”
If you’re the kind of coffee shop that sells out every morning, you’re doing something right. The only way to keep doing it is to keep doing it. Keep making the same coffee. Keep offering the same service. And if you must expand, try to expand into something bigger that can still offer the same, small-town experience.
The demand was just too big. That’s a great problem to have — but it’s still a problem. Don’t let success get to your head. Stay humble. Keep doing your thing. And remember that the best thing you can do for your customers is to give them more of what they already love about you.

### Title: Don’t Check Your Analytics

### Content: 
Yesterday, I checked my blog analytics so I could share last year’s 10 most popular posts based on views. I learned some lessons, but first, here they are:
’top 10 posts of 2022
- The 3 Kinds of Productivity You Need to Master
- 15 Things I Wish I Had Known When I Was 15
- How to Find Your Passion: 3 Exercises to Help You Figure Out Your True Calling
- The 7 Habits of Highly Successful People: A Summary of Stephen R. Covey’s Bestseller
- The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: A Summary of Stephen R. Covey’s Bestseller
- 5 Paradoxes of Life That’ll Make You Smarter
- 4 Stoic Lessons on Living the Good Life
- 8 Things To Do When Life Sucks
- 6 Stoic Exercises to Develop Self-Discipline
- The 4 Burners Theory of Work-Life Balance
Looking at this list, I learned several things. First, I can see that my most popular posts are the ones that are also most likely to be useful to the reader. The ones that provide a clear benefit, like inspiration, motivation, or a solution to a problem. Second, I noticed that a lot of list posts are up there. Third, I saw that the titles of those posts are usually pretty straightforward. They’re not clickbaity, but they’re clear and concise. Finally, I realized that a lot of my most popular posts are older ones, and that newer posts that have done well have done so because they’re similar in style to those older ones.
All of these lessons are valuable. I can use them to adjust my strategy. I can make more list posts, write more articles that are useful, and craft clearer titles. But I also learned something else: Checking your analytics is a lot of fun. It’s hard to stop once you begin. It’s easy to spend hours combing through the data, looking for patterns and insights. And it’s tempting to use those insights to justify a complete overhaul of your strategy.
But the truth is that the only thing you really need to do is keep writing. You don’t need to check your analytics every day, or even every week. You don’t need to know exactly how many views each post is getting, or which ones are the most popular. All you need to do is keep writing. Keep creating. Keep sharing your work with the world.
So here’s my advice to you: Don’t check your analytics. Not too often, anyway. Don’t get lost in the sea of data. Don’t let the numbers dictate your every move. Just keep doing your best work, and trust that the rest will fall into place.

### Title: Inbox as Insurance

### Content: 
My inbox keeps warning me that my storage is near its limit. Of course, Google would prefer I throw some money at the problem. “Just pay us $30/year, and we’ll give you more digital space!” I usually react by relentlessly deleting old files, but here, I’m tempted—because email is different.
Your inbox is a form of insurance. It’s not a policy you pay for, but it sure is one you should maintain. You don’t want to lose your email, and you don’t want to lose any of the information in it. I’ve had my Gmail address for 14 years. That’s a lot of data. A lot of connections. A lot of memories. I don’t want to lose any of those.
If you run a business, email is your lifeblood. It’s where you do deals, where you form relationships, and where you keep the receipts. I’ve had my business email for almost nine years. It, too, contains a wealth of information I don’t want to lose.
It’s easy to scoff at the idea of paying $2.50 per month for a little extra peace of mind, but if you’re serious about your business, your art, or your work, it’s a price you should be happy to pay. In fact, you should be looking for more insurance you can buy. What else can you do to protect your work?
I’ve been backing up my writing on Medium for years. I keep copies of my articles on my website, on my laptop, and on the cloud. I have an email newsletter, and I use a separate tool to make sure I can still email everyone if the primary one goes down. None of this is perfect, but it makes me feel better.
Your inbox is just one of many insurance policies you can buy for your business, but it’s an important one. Don’t let it slip through your fingers just because it feels like a small expense.

### Title: Be Early, or Don’t Be at All

### Content: 
In 2019, I posted every day on Substack for four months straight. My newsletter went from 0 to 4,000 subscribers. It was 100% organic growth with almost zero promotion.
-end-of-the-year-reflecting, I realized: The only way I could have grown my newsletter faster is to post twice a day. I was already posting daily. I was already doing the max I could do in terms of output. The only way to do more was to do more of the same.
That’s not a good sign. It’s a sign you’re doing it wrong. I was posting daily because I was scared. I was afraid that if I didn’t, people would forget me. I was afraid that if I didn’t, I’d lose readers. I was afraid that if I didn’t, my growth would stop. But I was also afraid that if I didn’t, I’d lose the momentum I had. I’d break the chain of daily posts, and I wouldn’t be able to get back on the horse.
I was right. In 2020, I posted only twice a month. I lost readers. I lost growth. I lost momentum. But I also gained a lot. I gained time. I gained energy. I gained peace of mind. I learned that it’s okay to take breaks. That you don’t have to do everything all the time. I learned that you can recover from almost anything. Even if you lose half your readers, you can still get them back. Or not. You can find new ones. You can reinvent yourself. You can change your mind.

### Title: The Kite and the Line

### Content: 
The Crain family is anything but a normal family, mostly because they lived in an anything-but-normal house. At one point in the spooky TV series telling their tale, however, the estranged father Hugh shares some advice with his son that works just as well for normal people as it does for those haunted by the ghosts of the past: If you’re a kite, find your line—and vice versa.
In the case of the kite, the line is the person who keeps it grounded yet allows it to soar at the same time. For the line, the kite is the person who keeps them humble and reminds them to enjoy life. The kite can’t fly without the line, and the line can’t have any fun without the kite.
Hugh was the kite, and his wife Olivia was the line. His daughter Shirley is the line for her husband Kevin, and so on. Some Crains are kites, others are lines, and finding the right partner can make all the difference in the world. Of course, the Crains are far from the only ones who need to get their matching elements in place in order to thrive.
If you’re a kite, find your line. If you’re a line, find your kite. The wind may be strong, and the ghosts may try to get you, but if you hold on to one another, you can achieve even the most seemingly impossible things.

### Title: Experiences Don’t End

### Content: 
Yesterday, I met someone at a party who, as it turned out, was in my year during undergrad. Same college. Same classes. Same exams. “Oh, but you must have never studied at the library then,” she said. “Actually, I was in the library all the time, often from 7 AM to 10 PM,” I responded. “Ahh, that’s why—I always went at night!”
What we learned from that interaction is that you can be in the same place at the same time as someone, and yet, have two completely different experiences. The library during the day is a busy, bustling place. People chat, laugh, eat, and try to study in groups. At night, it’s quiet, almost meditative. The few people who are there are serious about work, and the silence is palpable.
Experiences don’t end when we do. Just because we leave the library, the movie theater, or our friend’s house does not mean the people who were there with us no longer exist. They’re still there, living their lives. It’s the same when we leave a place: The experience continues without us.
You can’t change what you don’t know, but it helps to remember that the reality you see is not the only one that exists —and that what feels like the end is often just a new beginning for someone else.

### Title: Anxiety Blankets

### Content: 
Asked why he went back to drinking coffee after living without it for 30 days and seeing many benefits, Tim Ferriss said : “I use coffee as a security blanket when my life gets hit with something unpredictable or things seem a little out of control. So even though I realize, intellectually, that it’s counterproductive […], my response to feeling a little anxious is to want coffee—even though it increases anxiety physiologically.”
It’s a good thing to realize you’re using an anxiety blanket, and it’s a great next step to want to get rid of it. But if you’re a human performance athlete like Ferriss, you might want to consider a third option: making your anxiety blanket work for you instead of against you.
I’ve had a coffee a day habit for 15 years. It’s not perfect, but it’s also not so bad. I can go without for a day or two when I need to, but I’ve also learned that coffee can be a productive crutch. When I’m anxious, I can have a coffee and get rolling, and when I’m tired, I can have a coffee and get rolling. It’s a habit that’s always available to me, and I can rely on it to change my state.
If you’ve ever had a cigarette, a beer, or a cup of coffee to calm yourself down, you know anxiety blankets are real. The question is what are you going to do with yours? Will you try to get rid of it? Swap it for a better one? Or turn it into a springboard that’ll help you bounce back when you fall?
Your anxiety blankets are as unique as you are. There’s no one right answer. The important part is to realize you’re holding on to one. Or two. Or three. From there, you can make tradeoffs. Sacrifice one habit for another. Drop your anxiety blanket altogether, or turn it into a useful tool.
There’s a saying that “ everything you need is already inside.” That’s true, but it doesn’t hurt to look around your environment. You never know what you might find.

### Title: Relevant Notifications

### Content: 
When the Pokémon hype gets real, trying to buy new card sets throws me right back to the 90s. Except instead of driving to a store on release day, hoping to get some product, I’m checking various Discord servers and online shops ten times a day. “Is it live yet?” Naturally, I often end up missing the five-minute window in which listings go up and immediately sell out.
, for a collector, feel like the end of the world. But they’re not. I’m still here. The world is still turning. And the next set will be out soon enough. Still, I can’t help but think there must be a better way.
A few weeks ago, I discovered a tool that allows you to set up custom web alerts. You can track any website for changes, and if the tool detects any, it’ll send you an email. I set up a tracker for one of the shops I was following, and the peace of mind was instantaneous.
Instead of constantly fretting about missing a release, I could go about my day, knowing I’d get an email as soon as the cards were available. Of course, the listings still sold out within minutes, but at least now, I could try to be there for the drop without wasting hours of my life.
The tool is not perfect. It sometimes sends multiple emails for the same update. But it taught me a valuable lesson: Relevant notifications are worth their weight in gold.
There’s a saying that “ ignorance is bliss,” and while that’s true, it’s also a double-edged sword. We might not know what we’re missing, but we also can’t appreciate what we have.
In the case of Pokémon cards, I know what I’m missing, and that’s why relevant notifications help me. But in other areas, I’d rather just ignore the whole thing altogether. I don’t need to know how much my stocks are worth every day. I don’t need to know how many followers I have lost on any given day. And I don’t need to know who just published a new article on Medium.
The beauty of modern tools is that you can customize them to only deliver relevant notifications. Unfollow people on social media whose posts don’t add value. Filter your inbox so only important emails show up in your primary folder. And set up alerts for the websites you care about most.
In a world where information is always available, the best way to stay calm is to only engage when it matters. Design your notification system accordingly, and you’ll have the energy you need to do what counts.

### Title: Early Following Is Leading

### Content: 
In 2010, Derek Sivers gave a short-and-sweet TED talk that changed my understanding of leadership forever. Showing a short clip of a shirtless guy dancing by himself at a music festival, Derek explains: “First, a leader needs the guts to stand out and be ridiculed.” Well, that part I knew. It’s the part every movie, book, interview, and case study explains over and over again.
But then, a second guy joins the first one. He keeps dancing too. And then a third. And then a fourth. And within 30 seconds, the entire hill is flooded with people, all dancing, all having fun. “The first follower is what transforms the lone nut into a leader,” Derek says. “If the leader had the secret desire to be surrounded and accepted, he ends up surrounded and accepted. But it was the first follower who transformed the lone nut into a leader.”
This part I didn’t know. I’m not sure anyone does. We always say “leadership,” but we mostly talk about the lone nut, the person who stands out, the one who has to be bold, daring, and brave. But what about the followers? What about their role in all this? As it turns out, it is followers who turn leadership into what it is. “When you find a lone nut doing something great, have the guts to be the first person to stand up and join in,” Derek says.
Now, 13 years later, Derek gave an update on the talk. It’s a little longer, but the message is just as clear: “Early following is leading.” The first follower turns the lone nut into a leader, but the second follower is also important. “The second follower proves it’s really a movement,” Derek says. The third and fourth followers will make it look like it’s “more fun to be in it than to be on the sidelines.”
Derek also explains that the first followers will be the first leaders of the movement. “They’re the ones who are going to lead the way in teaching other people how to do it,” he says. “They’re the ones who are going to lead the way in organizing the group, in keeping it going, in spreading the word, and in taking it to the next level.”
It’s great to be a lone nut, to stand up for what you believe in. But it’s not the only way to lead. Early following is also leading. If you’re not the one who’s willing to look stupid, perhaps you can be the one who’s willing to look stupid for supporting someone who looks stupid. That, too, is a service.
As Derek says: “If you’re the first person to stand up and follow, you’re the leader of the followers. So early following is leading.”

### Title: Connecting Is Leading

### Content: 
My friend Mike hates giving presentations. He doesn’t enjoy being the center of attention in a group of people. He’d also be the last to volunteer to do role plays at work. Despite this, nobody I know would hesitate to call Mike a leader. In his own words, he just “ leads from behind.”
Mike does not have to stand in front of a crowd to inspire people. He does it by showing up to their cubicle, asking them how they’re doing, and really listening to the answer. He does it by remembering their partner’s name, their kids’ ages, and that they have a passion for mountain biking. And he does it by following through on his promises, showing up on time, and helping out wherever he can.
Mike doesn’t need to be a charismatic speaker to lead. He leads by connecting.
There’s a scene in the movie Hidden Figures in which a white man, Al Harrison, played by Kevin Costner, must give a speech to an all-Black team of “human computers” at NASA. The women are not exactly thrilled to listen to yet another white guy spew his vision, and so Harrison asks them to, in his words, “bear with him.”
After a few lines, however, he says something interesting: “I think there’s a picture very much worth a thousand words. I think you can judge a person’s character by what they do when they’re your equal, and I think you can measure a society by how it treats those people who are different.” Harrison then walks to the door, turns around, and says: “I’ll be right back.”
He leaves the room, and for a moment, everyone is stunned. Then, one of the women, Mary, breaks the silence: “That’s the end of the speech?” Another, Dorothy, says: “He’s just gone.” “He’s just gone,” Mary repeats. “What do you think he meant?” “I don’t know,” Dorothy says, “but he’s not here, and that’s a start.”
Al Harrison may not be the most outspoken man, but he is a man of his word. He follows through on his promises, shows up on time, and helps out wherever he can. He does it for the people who work for him, and he does it for the people who work with him. Al Harrison is a leader because he connects.
Leading is not about standing in front of a crowd. It’s about being part of a group of people. A group of people who believe in a certain vision of the future, and who are willing to work together to make that future a reality. You can be the person who most clearly sees that vision, the one who most vividly describes it, or the one who most boldly charges towards it, but you can also be the one who makes sure everyone keeps their eyes on the prize, who keeps spirits up along the way, and who reminds everyone that, at the end of the day, we’re all equal players on one united team.
The ways of leading are endless, but the most important part of leading will always be connecting. Never underestimate those who “lead from behind.”

### Title: The 3 Kinds of Eternity

### Content: 
Harry, the antihero of Hermann Hesse’s Steppenwolf, suffers a prolonged, fundamental identity crisis. One idea that gives him comfort is the concept of eternity, which various supporting characters define anew for him in illustrious ways.
’t say that I’m not the same person I was twenty years ago. I know I’m not. But I still have the same face. So in that sense, I’m the same person. The outside world is still the same, too. I’m still here, and the world is still here. That’s eternity, right there.
Harry’s friend, the theater lady, is a hedonist through and through. She believes in living life to the fullest, seizing the day, and indulging in all kinds of pleasures. Her view of eternity is somewhat limited in scope, but it does have one thing going for it: It’s based on Harry’s everyday experiences. It’s practical.
The theater lady’s eternity is the kind we can see when we look into the mirror. It’s the kind we feel when we touch an ancient artifact or see a picture of our great-grandparents. It’s the kind we can access by venturing to nature, be it the desert, the mountains, or the sea.
This eternity is about our limited time on earth, about what we can do, see, and feel while we’re here, and how we choose to spend those precious hours. It’s a useful perspective because it makes eternity feel tangible and attainable. It gives us a reason to try hard, to do our best, and to savor the journey. It also makes us feel as if we have failed when we don’t, and that’s its main problem.
If I could be reborn, I would like to return as a tree — probably as a larch. Why a larch? Because larches are the most beautiful trees. They live to a great age, and every autumn, they turn a glorious golden brown before they’re covered in snow. Why a tree? Well, trees have a sense of community. They stick together. They know they have to stay together. They don’t try to get away from one another. They live together and they die together. I think that’s a beautiful thing.
Harry’s second mentor is a man who appears as a literal wolf at times. He is the yin to the theater lady’s yang. Where she is all about indulgence, he is about asceticism. He, too, offers a definition of eternity, and it, too, is somewhat narrow.
The wolf’s eternity is the kind we can glimpse when we stand in a forest full of ancient trees, or when we look at a skyscraper reaching for the skies. It’s the kind we can sense when we feel the wind on our skin or hear the birds sing in the morning. It’s the eternity of the natural world, and it’s a lot bigger than the theater lady’s — but it’s still not big enough.
The wolf’s eternity is about the planet, about the earth, the plants, the animals, and the humans on it. It’s about nature and its circle of life, about the universe’s incomprehensible laws, and about our tiny roles in a cosmic, infinite story. This perspective is larger than ours and, therefore, humbling. It allows us to accept that we are small and that we can’t do everything, which, ironically, makes us feel bigger and stronger. It also makes us feel powerless and insignificant, and that’s its main problem.
I’m a writer. I’ve written loads of stuff. I’ve written poems, and essays, and novels. I’ve written a whole bunch of things that have been published and read by thousands of people. And I’ve written a whole bunch of other things that no one will ever see. But everything I’ve written is still out there. It’s all still in the world. And even when I’m long gone, the things I’ve written will still exist. I think that’s a kind of eternity, too.
Harry’s third and final teacher is a literal mirror image of himself. He is the ultimate guide to the self, and his definition of eternity is the most abstract of them all.
The mirror’s eternity is the kind we can feel when we read a book, hear a song, or look at a painting made by someone who’s no longer alive. It’s the kind we can sense when we feel “seen” by a character in a movie, a piece of dialogue in a play, or a line in a poem. It’s the eternity of the human spirit, and it’s the biggest of the three.
The mirror’s eternity is about the human soul, about its desires, its dreams, and its aspirations. It’s about the human mind, about its ideas, its creations, and its imagination. It’s about what humans can do for each other, about how we can inspire one another, and how we can change each other’s lives. This perspective is the most empowering because it shows us we have agency. It allows us to believe in the power of our actions and the impact we can have on others. It also makes us feel that our agency is never enough, and that’s its main problem.
The theater lady’s eternity is about what you can do while you’re alive. The wolf’s eternity is about what you can witness while you’re alive. The mirror’s eternity is about what you can leave behind once you’re gone. Each perspective has its benefits and flaws, but together, they form a comprehensive picture of what it means to be eternal — and it’s a picture that can help us find peace.
When you’re feeling stressed about all the things you want to do, remember that life is big. When you’re feeling sad about all the things you’ll never get to see, remember that nature is bigger. And when you’re feeling anxious about all the things you want to leave behind, remember that the human spirit is the biggest.
That’s what eternity is about. It’s not about what you can do, see, or leave behind. It’s about understanding your place in the universe, and then living in harmony with that place. It’s about knowing that you are small, that you are big, and that you are part of something much larger than yourself. If you can find this balance, you’ll never be worried about living forever — because you’ll already be at peace with the fact that you won’t.

### Title: One Does Not Love Breathing

### Content: 
Scout is smart for her age. By the time she goes to school, she can already read. Her teacher, instead of being amazed, sees her as a threat—to the other children but also to herself. When she is told to “tell her father to stop teaching her at home,” which he never has, she realizes for the first time: “What I have is precious, and there are people out there who’d take it away from me.”
Scout is a character in Go Set a Watchman, a follow-up to Harper Lee’s classic, To Kill a Mockingbird. The latter is written from Scout’s point of view, the former is not, and so we get to see Scout through her father’s eyes. Atticus, a lawyer and single parent, is proud of his daughter. He wants her to be independent. He wants her to think for herself. “I want you to be exposed to some civilized ideas,” he says, “and use the ones that suit you.”
When he finds out that Scout has been taught to not read, to not think for herself, to not use her imagination and, worst of all, that she has complied with these demands, he is furious. “When I was your age, I went through a brief period of intellectual curiousity, and I found myself invariably in the library because I simply didn’t know what I wanted to read. I read everything I could get my hands on, and I don’t think it did me any harm.”
Atticus knows what Scout’s teacher doesn’t: Once you’ve learned to think, you can’t unlearn it. It’s a gift you can’t return. “I can’t tell you what it was, but I found myself reading things that set the garden on fire for me. I’d never thought about these things, never wondered about them one way or another. But that’s what you do when you read—learn to see.”
Scout is glad to hear it. She is relieved. “I’m not alone any more,” she thinks. But there’s something else. Something Atticus says that, above all, makes her feel understood: “One doesn’t love breathing.” When we’re born, we’re thrust into a world we don’t know, and breathing is the first thing we must do to survive. From that moment on, we never think about it. It just happens. It’s an automatic function. In a way, so is thinking.
It’s true. Breathing is not something we do to feel alive. It’s a necessity. Something we must do to keep living. Similarly, thinking is not an indulgence. It’s not something we can turn on and off like a light switch. Thinking is our default state. Our natural way of moving through life. It’s what we do, and we can’t unlearn how to do it. We can only learn to do it better.
“Being a lawyer is kind of like being a doctor,” Atticus says. “You try to help whom you can, and you trust your instinct.” “I’m glad you’re a lawyer,” Scout says, “and I wish you’d been one all my life.” “I wish I had been too,” Atticus responds. “I’m not a very good one, but I do my best.” And then, once again, he reminds her: “One doesn’t love breathing.”
When you find yourself in a world that wants you to stop thinking, remember: One does not love breathing. You don’t have to justify your curiosity, your imagination, or your desire to see the world clearly. You only have to keep breathing. Thinking is part of the deal, and no one can take that from you.

### Title: Two Hamsters in the Background

### Content: 
We had some friends over for coffee and cake. Instead of just playing music from a speaker, I put on a lo-fi mix on our TV. Like most music videos of this kind, it featured a drawn wallpaper image. In the background, there were two cute hamsters, sitting, sipping tea from their cups.
’t a small detail, but it made the video — and thus our afternoon — a lot more fun. It’s amazing what little bits of creativity can do, and it’s important to remember that it’s often the tiniest bits that make the difference.
Don’t be afraid to add a little spark. You never know who might spot your two hamsters in the background, and even if no one does, you’ll still have a smile on your face.

### Title: Nothing Is True, Everything Is Permitted

### Content: 
Thus goes the creed of the Assassins, a secret organization sworn to protect humanity’s ability to choose. Whereas the Templars would rather do away with free will and keep the world at peace by putting it to sleep, the Assassins insist on their right to make mistakes and live with the consequences—for better or for worse.
 “Everything is permitted” sounds dangerous, even reckless, it is actually the Assassins’ dedication to this principle that keeps them in check. For the most part, they don’t go around killing people left, right, and center. They are assassins, yes, but they only assassinate targets they believe to be a true threat to the freedom of mankind. They even have a code: “Stay your blade from the innocent. Hide in plain sight. Never compromise the Brotherhood.”
The Assassins are well-aware of the power they wield, and they use it responsibly. They know they can assassinate anyone, anywhere, anytime, but they don’t. They only strike when they believe it matters. When they believe it is the right thing to do. That’s why “Nothing is true” is the more important half of their maxim. It allows them to change their mind at any second, and it keeps them from acting on false assumptions.
If nothing is true, then everything is up for debate. The Assassins don’t care about your opinion, but they will gladly adjust their behavior if you can prove them wrong. “Nothing is true” is a call to stay humble, to stay open-minded, and to keep looking for the truth. It’s a reminder that the truth is always changing, and that we must keep working on our own story and the story we tell about the world.
“Everything is permitted” is a corollary of “Nothing is true.” If there is no truth, then there can be no rules. No ethics. No morality. At least not in an absolute sense. It is up to us to create these things. To make our own rules. To live by our own ethics. To choose our own morals. “Everything is permitted” is a call to do so responsibly. To set boundaries for ourselves. To create our own code. And to only break it when we absolutely must.
The Assassins are a fictional organization, but their creed is as real as it gets. We can choose whatever we want to do, and we can change our minds whenever we want to change them. We are the ones writing the story of our lives. The only question is: What will we write in our next chapter?

### Title: Wooden Boxes

### Content: 
Last summer, I went for a hike. At the top of the mountain, there was the obligatory hut for rest and nourishment, but also a tiny chapel. I went inside and, on the left-hand wall, there was a wooden box. Kind of like a picture frame, but deeper, and with a simple pane of glass to protect its contents.
In it, there were a few stones, a piece of wood, and a little plastic figurine of a deer. It was the kind of display you might see in a museum, except this one wasn’t behind thick glass and came without a description. I looked at it for a while. I thought about what it might mean, and I concluded that, like all art, it meant nothing and everything at the same time.
I was reminded of this box when I saw a picture of another one. My friend Zulie shared it in a Slack channel. The box was also made of wood, but instead of a display, it was a simple container. On the lid, using the same kind of letters you might find on a pinboard, it simply said, “Things I Will Not Apologize For.”
Zulie said she wanted to make one. “It will hold all the things that I’m proud of, that I’m not sorry for, and that I won’t apologize for. I’ll keep it somewhere where I can see it every day, and it’ll give me strength.”
I love this idea. I think I’ll make one too. I’m not sure yet what I’ll put in it, but I do know it’ll be the kind of art that makes you think. Just like that other wooden box on top of a mountain, which, actually, it will be.

### Title: A Good Play To Act Out

### Content: 
In the video game Crisis Core, one of the main characters, Genesis, is obsessed with a poem titled Loveless. Thanks to the developers’ creative efforts, the five-act ballad is a full-fledged piece of art, both in English and Japanese, and it has been featured in Final Fantasy game releases spanning almost 30 years.
In the game, Genesis quotes the poem at various times, and he does so again just before he leaves the player’s side for a while. “I am the snake that tempts mankind to taste forbidden knowledge,” he says. “I am the apple that brought sin and punishment into the world.” Genesis is referring to the story of Adam and Eve, the first humans, who ate from the Tree of Life against God’s command. As a result, they were expelled from paradise, and, from that day forward, humanity was both capable of and prone to sinning.
“Their eyes were opened, and they knew good and evil,” Genesis continues. “The light of knowledge will reach even the darkest of corners.” And then, with a final line, he leaves the player’s side: “I am the wind blowing through the devil’s mask. I am the shadow swaying in the darkness.”
When we play games, we become the main character. We are the ones venturing into the dark, and we are the ones meant to carry the light of knowledge. We are the wind blowing through the devil’s mask, and we are the shadow swaying in the darkness. We are the snake that tempts mankind to taste forbidden knowledge, and we are the apple that brought sin and punishment into the world.
If you’re not a gamer, this might sound like gibberish, but if you are, you know what I’m talking about. You’ve felt the weight of the world on your shoulders, and you’ve carried it. You’ve brought light into the darkness, and you’ve slain the shadow. You’ve eaten from the Tree of Life, and you’ve saved the world.
Of course, the world isn’t a video game, and so the stakes are different. There is no final boss, no ending, and no easy path to salvation. But there is a light of knowledge, and it does reach even the darkest of corners. There is a snake that tempts us to taste forbidden knowledge, and there is an apple that brings sin and punishment into the world. We might not always be the ones holding the torch, but we are all part of the grand story.
The next time you feel lost, confused, or hopeless, remember: You are not alone. You are not the only one. You are not the only one struggling, the only one failing, the only one who feels like they can’t get it right. You are not the only one who feels lonely, who feels like they don’t belong, who feels like they’re not good enough. You are not the only one who feels like they’re not worthy, who feels like they’re not deserving, who feels like they’re not lovable. You are not the only one who feels like they’re not strong enough, who feels like they’re not smart enough, who feels like they’re not capable enough. You are not the only one who feels like they’re not good enough, who feels like they’re not worthy enough, who feels like they’re not deserving enough.
You are the snake that tempts mankind to taste forbidden knowledge. You are the apple that brought sin and punishment into the world. You are the wind blowing through the devil’s mask. You are the shadow swaying in the darkness. You are the light of knowledge, and you will reach even the darkest of corners. You are the hero of your own story, and you will save the world.

### Title: Delete the Adjectives, Get the Facts

### Content: 
Cool-headed as she is, Scout Finch cannot escape every trap life sets for any child growing up with a four years older brother. By the time Jem hits sixth grade, he actually gets interested in what school has to offer. Unfortunately for Scout, whatever he learns he blows out of proportion when relaying it to her.
’times, Jem said, I don’t see why he can’t behave like other people’s dads. “What other people?” “Well, like Mr. Avery.” “Mr. Avery’s a Methodis t,” said Jem. “He won’t let his children do anything. Methodists don’t believe in having fun. He’s against automobiles for one thing.”
“Why?” “Well, I reckon because he’s a foot-washing Baptist. They don’t believe in cars or newspapers either.” “Where’d you get all this?” “From Miss Maudie. Methodists just have church, that’s all.” “Well, if Methodists don’t like to take their fun, I’ve no use for ’em,” I said. “They sure have funny ways.”
Jem said Mr. Avery misinterpreted some scripture when he told Miss Maudie God said it was an abomination for women to wear pants.
“Why, that’s not in the Bible,” I said.
“Jem, what in the sam hill are a methodist and a baptist?”
“Methodists go to church on Sunday, just like everybody else,” said Jem. “But they like to have fun, too, so they go to evening church on Monday, to make up for it.”
“I thought the Methodists went to church at night.”
“That’s the Holiness,” Jem said. “They’re even newer than the Methodists.”
I imagined a beautiful church, with a red velvet carpet, where the proud organist swept his hands up and down the mighty keyboard, and the congregation raucously sang “Onward, Christian Soldiers.”
The Holiness seemed far superior to the Methodists: “How holy are they?”
“Methodists are like that, too,” Jem said. “They like to have fun. They just don’t show it so much.”
“Are Methodists and Holiness the same?”
“No, the Holiness are the ones that say ‘Hallelujah, Jesus’ and all like that.”
“Where did you get all this?”
“From Miss Maudie.”
“Did you ask her?”
“No, Scout, it’s something you’re born with. Every Methodist I ever saw was either born in the Methodist or married one.”
“Are you a Methodis t?”
“Naw, I ain’t anything. I just go to church when they tell me to. Are you a Methodis t?”
“Hell, no. I ain’t nothin’ either.”
I had a feeling that Jem and I would get along even better now that our childhood differences were practically wiped out. We would be much more alike, and it was Jem’s turn to learn a hard lesson.
As a nine-year-old boy, Jem is just as prone to fall for stereotypes as any other kid. It’s a natural reflex to simplify the world so we can understand it, and it’s on us to eliminate our adjectives as we grow up. Jem’s only problem is that he’s so eager to share his newfound “knowledge” with his sister, and Scout Finch is anything but gullible.
Like a fisher pulling in her catch, she questions Jem’s assertions one by one. “Where’d you get all this?” “Why?” “Well, if Methodists don’t like to take their fun, I’ve no use for ’em,” she says. “They sure have funny ways.” It’s not that Scout is immune to prejudice, it’s just that she’s too curious to not ask questions. She’d rather have the facts, and if there are none to be had, she’ll make up her own mind — or make up her own story, like the image of a beautiful church she conjures next.
It’s not a bad thing to fill in the gaps when reality won’t give us the answers we seek. In fact, it’s a wonderful human ability. What’s important is that we do it deliberately, and that we return to filling in the gaps once we do get the real information we need. As long as we keep digging for the truth, we can wear our bias like a coat, putting it on when we need it and taking it off when we don’t.
Scout’s relentless questioning, however, does have one victim: Jem. “I had a feeling that Jem and I would get along even better now that our childhood differences were practically wiped out,” Scout notes. “We would be much more alike, and it was Jem’s turn to learn a hard lesson.” What’s that lesson? “It’s never too late to start over,” Jem will claim later in the book. And while that’s true, there’s also this: “Every Methodist I ever saw was either born in the Methodist or married one.” No matter how hard we try, we’ll never be free of bias completely — but as long as we’re willing to admit it, that’s okay.
Don’t worry about your adjectives so much. Delete them when you can, but when you can’t, don’t be afraid to make up your own ending. Just remember to return to the real story later, and don’t get too carried away when you’re sharing it with others.

### Title: Writing on Graph Paper

### Content: 
On yesterday’s train, a teacher sat across my table. He was grading a history exam. The students’ longhand writing and little notes he left reminded me of my time in school.
’ts in the margins, pointing at the right answers. “Yes! This is correct.” “No! Wrong.” Some questions had more than one “Yes!” because multiple statements were true. Others had several “No!”s, indicating the student had gotten everything wrong.
I don’t remember the last time I wrote on graph paper, but I do remember that the teacher’s notes on my exams were always my favorite part. It’s the kind of feedback you can’t get when you write online. It’s the kind of feedback that makes you feel seen.
In an online world where the data is always available, where every piece of writing can be tracked, measured, and analyzed in real-time, it’s easy to feel like a faceless cog in a giant, soulless machine. But you’re not. You’re a human, and your writing is worth more than the price of milk. It’s not just a commodity, and we don’t just skim the top for cream.
Every day, millions of people read your work. Most of them will never comment. But that doesn’t mean they don’t see you. They might not tell you, but they still leave little notes in the margins. “Yes! This is correct.” “No! Wrong.” Sometimes, they’ll highlight a line or circle a paragraph. They might even cut out a piece and pin it to their wall.
You’re not writing on graph paper, but your writing is still seen. You’re not alone, and you’re not writing into the void. Keep going — and remember that, unlike in a high school history class, there are no wrong answers.

### Title: The Water Cathedral of Identity

### Content: 
Modern books are often littered with testimonials. My copy of Der Steppenwolf by Hermann Hesse needs just one: “There are only few books which transform us, which give us courage to change our lives,” French writer Frederic Beigbeder says on the back cover. “ Der Steppenwolf is one such book.”
In the novel, a man named Harry Haller finds a mysterious book in the streets. The title? “Treatise on the Steppenwolf.” As he reads it in his small attic, he realizes it is an exact description of himself, his life, and his struggles. The book is split into three parts, and while the first two offer some historical context and a glimpse into Harry’s everyday life, the third is what truly earns the book its transformative reputation.
After a magical night at a lavish party, Harry finds himself in a place that feels like a dream. He wanders the streets, and suddenly, a door appears. The door leads into a building, and in the building, there is a library. As Harry browses the shelves, he finds book after book about himself. Each one is titled “Harry Haller’s Records,” and each one seems to tell a different story. One describes him as a man of the world, another as a thinker, and yet another as a musician.
Harry is confused. How can there be so many books about him, each one so different from the next? Eventually, he realizes: “I was a picture of manifoldness and disharmony, but also of oneness and harmony. I was a collection of opposites, held together only by the most vulnerable and delicate tie: the tie of a body, a soul, and a mind.”
As he continues to browse, Harry spots a book that seems to hold the key to the entire library: “The Magic Theater — Not for Everybody.” Intrigued, he opens it, and suddenly, he hears a voice. It is the voice of Hermes, the messenger of the gods, and it will guide Harry through the rest of his journey.
Hermes explains to Harry that the library is not just a library. It is a place of infinite selves. A water cathedral of identity. “Every man has a thousand lives, and every man loses a thousand lives,” Hermes says. “But every man also wins a thousand lives, and every man is a thousand men.”
Harry is skeptical. He doesn’t understand how this can be. Hermes reminds him that every human is a universe in their own right, and that the universe is infinite. Therefore, every human is also infinite. “You are a universe of universes, Harry,” Hermes says. “You are a star among stars, a sun among suns. You are a god among gods, a devil among devils. You are a hero among heroes, a villain among villains. You are a saint among saints, a sinner among sinners. You are a man among men, a woman among women. You are a child among children, an adult among adults. You are a boy among boys, a girl among girls. You are a father among fathers, a mother among mothers. You are a son among sons, a daughter among daughters. You are a friend among friends, an enemy among enemies. You are a lover among lovers, a hater among haters. You are a winner among winners, a loser among losers. You are a teacher among teachers, a student among students. You are a master among masters, a servant among servants. He can choose any door he likes, and explore any world he wants.
Harry is overwhelmed. He doesn’t know where to start. Hermes smiles and says: “The choice is yours, Harry. But remember, every door leads to a new adventure, a new self, a new life. And every adventure, every self, every life is worth living.”
